overview: Ameren is a St. Louis-based public utility holding company whose primary assets are its equity interests in Union Electric Company (d/b/a Ameren Missouri), Ameren Illinois Company, and Ameren Transmission Company of Illinois (ATXI). Ameren Missouri operates rate-regulated electric generation, transmission, and distribution and a rate-regulated natural gas distribution business in Missouri; Ameren Illinois operates rate-regulated electric transmission, electric distribution, and natural gas distribution businesses in Illinois; ATXI operates a FERC-regulated electric transmission business within MISO. The company reports in four segments -- Ameren Missouri, Ameren Illinois Electric Distribution, Ameren Illinois Natural Gas, and Ameren Transmission -- and is listed on the NYSE.

business_model.summary: Ameren earns a regulated return on and of capital invested in rate base (electric generation/transmission/distribution and natural gas distribution infrastructure) as set by the Missouri Public Service Commission (MoPSC), the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC), and FERC. Revenue is overwhelmingly cost-of-service/rate-base driven -- almost all of Ameren's revenues are subject to state or federal rate regulation -- making it highly recurring and non-discretionary (essential electric and gas service to captive franchise customers), with upside tied to rate base growth, allowed ROEs, and incremental large-load/data-center demand rather than volume or pricing competition.
business_model.customer_type: Regulated franchise service to residential, commercial, and industrial retail customers, plus a fast-growing large-load/data-center industrial customer class under new large-load tariffs
business_model.geographic_mix: Missouri (Ameren Missouri service territory, including St. Louis) and Illinois (Ameren Illinois service territory, central and southern Illinois); FY2025 segment revenue of $8,799M split roughly $4,795M Ameren Missouri, $2,399M Ameren Illinois Electric Distribution, $968M Ameren Illinois Natural Gas, $862M Ameren Transmission (before intersegment eliminations)

competitive_position.market_position: Sole regulated electric/gas distribution utility within its exclusive Missouri and Illinois franchise territories; not a market-share business in the traditional sense since it holds a legal monopoly on wires/pipes in its service area, though it competes with other utilities and independent power producers for siting new large industrial/data-center loads and competes for capital with electric transmission projects awarded competitively through MISO

moat_factors.description: Exclusive legal right to serve native-load retail customers in its Missouri and Illinois territories; new entrants cannot duplicate wires/pipes infrastructure

Allowed to earn a regulator-approved return on and of invested capital (WACC on rate base), providing predictable, recurring cash flows largely insulated from volume risk via decoupling mechanisms (RBA, VBA) and cost trackers (FAC, PGA, PISA, RESRAM)
Investment-grade credit ratings and access to $3.2B of multiyear credit facilities and a $5B ATM equity program support a historically large, and growing, capital program
Missouri's PISA/RESRAM and Illinois' MYRP/RBA/VBA reduce (but do not eliminate) regulatory lag between capital spend and rate recovery

weaknesses: No pricing power or ability to grow outside the rate-base/ROE framework set by regulators -- all growth must be approved by the MoPSC, ICC, and FERC

Two-state regulatory exposure (Missouri and Illinois) creates jurisdictional risk -- outcomes, allowed ROEs (Illinois electric 8.72%, Illinois gas 9.60%, transmission 10.48% vs. Missouri's higher-ROE-but-less-transparent framework) and reconciliation caps differ materially and are subject to appeal
Heavy reliance on continuous equity issuance (DRPlus, ATM program, forward sales) to fund the capital plan, which dilutes EPS growth per share even as rate base compounds

Coal generation (Labadie, Sioux) still ~5% of Ameren's and ~11% of Ameren Missouri's rate base, exposing the company to environmental compliance costs and stranded-asset risk as retirements are phased to 2042

Data center/large-load pipeline is large but largely unexecuted -- actual materialization timing (2027 and beyond) and realized demand could fall short of the signed 2.8 GW / additional 1.2+ GW under construction agreements

growth_drivers: Rate base growth driven by a rapidly rising capital investment plan -- most recently $38.1 billion of planned infrastructure investment (2027-2031 guidance base) and an estimated up to $46.0 billion of capex from 2026 through 2031 per the Q3-2026 10-Q, versus $30.5-33.1B for 2026-2030 disclosed in the FY2025 10-K -- implying ~13.3% compounded annual rate base growth 2026-2031

Large-load/data-center demand: Ameren Missouri signed electric service agreements for 2.8 GW of demand (expected to begin materializing in H2 2027, full capacity by 2030), plus construction agreements for an additional ~1.2-3.4 GW and several more GW in interconnection studies; Google and Amazon projects reportedly represent ~$25B of related investment

Ameren Missouri's September 2026 preferred resource plan targets 2.9 GW of load growth by 2030, 5 GW by 2035, and 6 GW by 2045, with large additions of natural gas (combined-cycle and simple-cycle), solar, wind, battery storage, natural gas fuel cells, and up to 1,200 MW of new nuclear generation by 2040

MISO long-range transmission plan awards to Ameren and ATXI (first and second tranche projects, plus newly awarded competitive-bid projects in 2026) add FERC-regulated transmission rate base with constructive incentive ROEs (10.48% including RTO participation adder)
Grid modernization and reliability investment in both Missouri (Smart Energy Plan) and Illinois (Grid Plan/MYRP) support continued distribution rate base growth

Large-load tariff structure (approved November 2025, minimum billing at 80% of requested demand, 100% cost responsibility for large-load-driven infrastructure under Senate Bill 4/SB4) is designed to let data center growth subsidize, rather than burden, existing ratepayers -- supportive of constructive regulatory treatment
Long-term EPS growth guidance of 8-10% compounded annually (2027-2031, off a 2027 midpoint of $5.80), among the highest in the regulated utility peer group

business.description: Current EPS/capex guidance embeds only a fraction of the signed 2.8 GW pipeline (reported base case ~1.2 GW); if large-load customers delay or cancel projects, the capital plan and growth algorithm could be overbuilt relative to realized demand
Nearly all revenue is earned under MoPSC, ICC, and FERC frameworks; adverse rulings in either state materially affect consolidated earnings

business.risk: Execution risk on a rapidly scaling capital program
business.description: Plan has grown from ~$21-22.8B (2024-28) to up to $46.0B (2026-31) in roughly two years; project delays, cost overruns, supply chain/tariff pressure, and labor availability could impair returns on this much larger build

Labadie and Sioux coal retirements (2036/2042 and 2032) and natural gas unit retirements in Illinois (by 2040) carry stranded-asset, environmental compliance, and replacement-generation execution risk

financial.description: Total debt ~$19.2B against ~$13.5B of shareholders' equity; Ameren continues to issue significant new long-term debt (~$3.2B in 9M-2026) to fund capex, raising financing costs as noted in Q3-2026 MD&A

Diluted share count grew from ~269.9M to ~276.4M in a year via DRPlus, 401(k), and forward sale agreements; ~$5B of additional equity financing planned 2027-2031, which caps per-share growth even as the balance sheet and rate base expand
Capex and dividends are expected to exceed operating cash flow for the next several years, requiring continued external financing and sensitivity to capital-market access and cost

regulatory.risk: Pending Missouri electric rate case uncertainty
regulatory.description: June 2026 filing seeks a $343M annual revenue increase based on a 10.25% ROE ask, 52% equity ratio, and $16.7B rate base; MoPSC decision due by May 2027 with new rates effective June 2027 -- outcome and timing are not guaranteed

regulatory.risk: Illinois ROE and reconciliation cap risk
regulatory.description: Ameren Illinois' electric distribution MYRP (2024-2027) ROE of 8.72% and reconciliation cap are under appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court; outcomes of pending appeals (2025 natural gas rate order, 2024 MYRP order) are uncertain

regulatory.risk: FERC transmission incentive ROE policy risk
regulatory.description: A pending FERC rulemaking could eliminate the 50-basis-point RTO participation incentive ROE adder, which management estimates would reduce annual net income by an estimated $19M (Ameren) / $14M (Ameren Illinois) based on 2026 projected rate base
Clean Air Act, CCR Rule, and potential future greenhouse-gas regulation could require significant incremental capex or force earlier-than-planned coal/gas retirements, with uncertain cost recovery

macro.description: Heavy reliance on long-term debt and equity issuance to fund an enlarged capital plan makes Ameren sensitive to higher-for-longer rates, which raise financing costs and can pressure allowed ROEs (some Illinois mechanisms are explicitly tied to 30-year Treasury yields)

Results are affected by heating/cooling degree days; normal-weather assumptions underpin 2026/2027 guidance and deviations (either direction) move quarterly results, partially offset by weather-normalization and decoupling riders

Coal, nuclear fuel, natural gas, and purchased power costs are largely passed through via FAC, PGA, and similar trackers (95% of Missouri net energy cost variance), limiting -- but not eliminating -- margin risk

macro_factors.industry_outlook: US regulated electric/gas utilities are in a historically strong investment cycle driven by grid modernization, electrification, renewable/generation transition, and (new) data center/AI-driven load growth; Ameren is among the names most levered to the data center theme given Missouri's large-load tariff and signed hyperscaler-related agreements
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low -- regulated utility earnings are largely non-cyclical and defensive, insulated from economic cycles by rate-base economics and revenue decoupling, though large-load/data-center demand introduces a newer, less-tested growth variable
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High -- large, growing capital program funded with continuous debt and equity issuance; cost of capital directly affects financing costs and, in Illinois energy-efficiency mechanisms, the allowed ROE itself
key_input_costs: Materials/equipment for grid and generation buildout (transformers, turbines, battery storage, solar/wind components)

recent_developments.event: Ameren raised 2026 EPS guidance to $5.35-$5.55 (from $5.25-$5.45), issued 2027 EPS guidance of $5.70-$5.90, and introduced 8-10% compound annual EPS growth guidance for 2027-2031; capital plan guidance raised to $38.1 billion

Ameren Missouri filed its 2026 preferred resource plan (2026 PRP) with the MoPSC, targeting 2.9 GW of load growth by 2030 and 5 GW by 2035, adding gas, solar, wind, storage, and up to 1,200 MW of nuclear, while retiring all coal by 2042
Ameren Missouri filed for a $343 million annual electric rate increase based on a 10.25% requested ROE and $16.7 billion rate base; MoPSC decision expected by May 2027

Ameren Missouri acquired the Split Rail Solar Project (~$0.6 billion, 300 MW) and placed it in service by June 2026; large-load customers executed electric service agreements representing 2.8 GW of demand

MoPSC approved Ameren Missouri's new large-load customer rate structure/tariff (minimum billing at 80% of requested demand for customers ≥75 MW), designed to protect existing customers from data-center-driven cost increases

ICC issued an order on Ameren Illinois' natural gas delivery rate review, approving a $79 million annual revenue increase based on a 9.60% ROE and $3.2 billion rate base, effective December 2025; Ameren Illinois has since appealed aspects of the order

Missouri's Power Predictability and Reliability Act (PPRA) became effective, extending Ameren Missouri's PISA election through 2035 (extendable to 2040), enabling future test years for gas rate cases, and allowing construction-work-in-progress in rate base for new generation under integrated resource planning

Management transitions: Michael Moehn became Group President, Ameren Utilities and interim Chairman/President of Ameren Missouri; Leonard P. Singh became EVP and CFO of Ameren; Patrick Smith Sr. became Chairman/President of Ameren Illinois

items.notes: Raised from prior $5.25-$5.45 guidance, driven by infrastructure investment, large-load agreements, and favorable weather-normalized sales growth
Represents ~8.4% growth versus the original FY2026 guidance midpoint
New long-term growth algorithm range, among the highest of regulated utility peers, underpinned by the enlarged capital and rate base plan

items.target: $38.1 billion (2027-2031 guidance base); up to $46.0 billion disclosed for 2026-2031 in Q3-2026 10-Q
items.notes: Up materially from $30.5-33.1 billion (2026-2030) in the FY2025 10-K and $25.2-27.4 billion (2025-2029) in the prior plan; increase driven by Ameren Missouri's 2026 PRP and additional ATXI/MISO transmission projects
Reflects the larger capital program, including large-load-driven generation and transmission investment
Ameren expects to continue growing the common dividend annually within this payout range
Includes forward sale agreements under the $5B ATM program (increased from $3B in August 2026), DRPlus, and employee benefit plans; issuances concentrated near year-end 2027 and year-end 2028

guidance.management_commentary: Management frames the 2.8 GW of signed large-load electric service agreements (plus construction agreements for additional gigawatts) as largely incremental upside not yet fully embedded in guidance, while emphasizing disciplined cost management and the large-load tariff's cost-responsibility provisions to protect existing customers. Management continues to flag regulatory lag, pending rate case outcomes in Missouri and Illinois, and financing/equity needs as the principal risks to executing the enlarged capital plan.

bull_case: Data center/large-load demand (2.8 GW signed, additional gigawatts in construction agreements and interconnection studies, including reported Google/Amazon-linked projects) provides a multi-year rate base growth catalyst largely unique among Midwest regulated utilities

Industry-leading long-term EPS growth guidance of 8-10% (2027-2031) versus typical utility peer growth of 5-7%, supported by a capital plan that has roughly doubled over two years ($21-23B to up to $46B)

Constructive and improving regulatory mechanisms (Missouri's PPRA/PISA extension through 2035-2040, Illinois' MYRP, large-load tariff with 100% cost responsibility for data centers) reduce regulatory lag and protect base-rate customers from large-load risk
Diversified, de-risked cash flows: nearly all revenue is rate-regulated, with FAC/PGA/RBA/VBA mechanisms decoupling earnings from weather, volumes, and most commodity cost swings

Strong historical total shareholder return versus utility benchmarks (AEE cumulative TSR of 148 vs. S&P 500 Utility Index's 159 and Philadelphia Utility Index's 153 off a $100 base since 2020) with continued dividend growth within a 45-55% payout target
bear_case: Current EPS guidance reportedly embeds only a fraction (~1.2 GW) of the signed 2.8 GW data center pipeline; if large-load demand is delayed past 2027 or scaled back, the oversized capital plan risks being built ahead of realized revenue

Heavy and growing reliance on new equity (~$5B planned 2027-2031, plus ATM program expanded to $5B) dilutes per-share growth and signals the balance sheet cannot fund the capital plan from debt and internal cash flow alone
Pending Missouri rate case ($343M ask, 10.25% ROE) and Illinois appeals (MYRP ROE, 2025 gas rate order) create binary regulatory outcomes that could compress allowed returns versus plan assumptions

Rising leverage (~$19.2B total debt) and persistently negative free cash flow (capex plus dividends exceeding operating cash flow for years) leave Ameren exposed to higher-for-longer interest rates and credit-market access/pricing

Coal (Labadie, Sioux) and aging gas generation carry transition, stranded-asset, and environmental compliance risk, while an unprecedented pace of generation/transmission construction (gas, solar, wind, storage, nuclear life extension) raises execution risk across labor, supply chain, and permitting
